When you pelt someone or something, you throw things at them repeatedly, quickly, and with force. It's not a gentle toss. It's aggressive, rapid, and usually relentless — like an attack of throwing.

Think of it this way: if throwing a single stone at someone is throwing, then pelting is throwing ten stones at someone, one after another, fast and hard. The repetition and the force are what make it pelt.

The angry crowd pelted the car with eggs.
The kids pelted each other with snowballs.

Notice the structure: pelt + someone/something + with + the thing being thrown. That's the most natural way to use it.
What Makes It Different From Just "Throw"

This is important. You can throw a ball once, calmly, to a friend. That's neutral. But pelt carries extra meaning baked in:

  • Force — it's hard and fast, not soft or gentle
  • Repetition — it's not one throw, it's many
  • A target — you're always pelting at or with something, aimed at something specific

So if someone says "They pelted him with questions," you instantly understand that the questions came fast, hard, and without pause — like a bombardment. The word works figuratively too, not just literally.

Pelt is also used to describe rain, hail, or wind hitting something with great force and speed. Here, nothing is being "thrown" by a person — but the feeling is the same: something is striking a surface hard and rapidly.

Rain pelted the windows all night.
Hailstones pelted the roof.

You can almost hear the drumming, relentless impact in those sentences. This is a very natural and common use of the word.

Pelt has one more meaning that surprises many learners: it can mean to run or move at full speed.

She pelted down the street to catch the bus.
The dog pelted across the field.

Here, no throwing is involved at all. The word captures the idea of moving with urgency and explosive speed, like someone sprinting flat-out. This use is particularly common in British English. Context makes it very clear — if someone is pelting down a hallway, they're running fast, not throwing anything.

Across all its meanings, pelt always carries the same emotional energy: intensity, speed, and force. Whether someone is throwing things at you, rain is hammering the ground, or a person is sprinting wildly — there is nothing slow, mild, or controlled about it.

This is why pelt is such a vivid, punchy word. Writers use it when they want you to feel the relentless, rapid impact of something — not just know that it happened.
Quick Summary of All Three Uses

① Throw things forcefully and repeatedly at a target
→ The boys pelted the bully with water balloons.

② (Of rain, hail, etc.) to strike something hard and fast
→ Sleet pelted the windshield the entire drive home.

③ To run or move at full speed
→ He pelted across the room the moment he heard the news.

That is the complete picture of pelt as a verb — every meaning, every nuance, and the feeling it creates in a sentence.
